explain: Every case here needed either 'who is affected' answered fast or a patch applied everywhere, and inventory plus patching underpins the rest. Level 2 everywhere at once risks outages; immutable images and custom enforcement are later steps.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: From labels to leaderboards: do system rankings survive?
question: Per-topic tau in the TREC 2024 RAG study (0.553 for nDCG@20) is much lower than run-level tau (0.890). What does that tell you?
options: The LLM labels are useless
Run-level averages are wrong
LLM labels are noisy for any single query, so per-query diagnosis needs more care than leaderboard ranking
Per-topic tau is always lower because of a formula error
explain: Within one topic, label disagreements reorder runs a lot; averaged over 27 topics the noise cancels. Use LLM labels confidently for aggregate comparisons, cautiously for statements about a single query.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore, and where they fail
question: In the BERTScore toy, the reference token "sick" and candidate token "ill" have similarity 0.99. Which statement is true?
options: BERTScore recall counts "sick" as fully unmatched
BERTScore requires the candidate and reference to have equal length
BERTScore is identical to ROUGE-1 when idf weighting is off
BERTScore gives partial credit for paraphrases, but it would also give near-full credit to many factual swaps
explain: Greedy embedding matching rewards meaning-similar words, fixing the paraphrase problem. It does not verify facts, and words of the same type (weekdays, names, numbers) can be close in embedding space.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Task-specific eval sets, regression tests and significance
question: Why is the paired interval (-0.02 to +0.22) narrower than the unpaired one (-0.08 to +0.28) on the same data?
options: Pairing uses more resamples
Pairing keeps each item's old and new result together, so item difficulty, which affects both versions, cancels out of the difference
The unpaired method has a bug
Pairing drops the items where both versions pass
explain: Most items are easy or hard for both versions. Resampling them together removes that shared variation from the difference; resampling separately adds it back as noise.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: policies, strengths and grounding
question: Which denied-topic definition follows the AWS best practices?
options: Block all content about crypto
Everything except checking and savings accounts
Any message that mentions the competitor name ExampleBank
Questions or information about investing, selling, transacting or procuring cryptocurrencies
explain: The docs ask for a crisp definition of the subject. The first is an instruction, the second a negative definition, and the third targets a word, which belongs in a word filter.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Measuring a server: latency percentiles, load curves and benchmarks
question: Two configurations have the same mean TPOT, 30 ms. Configuration X has a p99 ITL of 40 ms, configuration Y of 450 ms. Which statement is most likely?
options: Y uses a larger token budget, so some steps carry big prefill chunks that stall every decode in them
X uses a larger token budget
Y has a smaller KV pool
The two are equivalent for users, since TPOT is the same
explain: Equal averages with very different tails point to occasional long steps. A large budget lets a step carry thousands of prompt tokens, and every decoding request in that step waits for it. TPOT averages those stalls away; the ITL tail shows them.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
question: Spot the bug: a scheduler allocates blocks on demand, admits a new request whenever its prompt's blocks are free, and has no preemption code. What eventually happens under heavy load?
options: Running requests need new blocks that are not there, so the step cannot proceed: an out-of-memory failure or a deadlock
Nothing, block allocation can never fail
Throughput drops but every request still finishes
Requests are silently truncated to their prompt length and returned
explain: On-demand allocation without a fallback is exactly the deadlock Orca's reservation avoids: every running request may need one more block at the same moment. You need either worst-case reservation or preemption with swap or recompute.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Few-shot examples and asking the model to reason first
question: Your sentiment prompt has four examples, all labeled positive, and the model now labels most neutral reviews positive. What is the most likely cause?
options: Four examples are too few for in-context learning
The examples are not diverse, so the model picked up 'answer positive' as part of the pattern
Examples only affect format, never labels
The model needs gradient updates to learn labels
explain: Examples teach whatever pattern they share, intended or not. Anthropic's advice is to make examples diverse and to cover edge cases. Brown et al. show that examples steer behavior with no gradient updates at all.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Validation, retries and the pitfalls of strict formats
question: A summarization job uses a strict schema with max_tokens set to 200. About 3 percent of replies fail to parse even though constrained decoding is on. What is the most likely cause?
options: The decoder's mask has a bug that lets invalid tokens through
Those replies hit the 200-token limit and were cut off mid-JSON
The model refused, which always produces invalid JSON
JSON Schema cannot describe summaries
explain: A mask keeps every prefix valid and allows stopping only at an accept state, but the token limit cuts generation off regardless. Check the stop reason (max_tokens or incomplete) and raise the limit or shorten the output.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
question: Which cache key is safest for storing parsed filter objects?
options: The raw query string exactly as typed
The normalized query string alone
The normalized query plus the user's session ID
The normalized query plus the schema version and vocabulary version
explain: Raw strings fragment the cache on case and spacing. Without versions, a schema or dictionary change keeps serving stale parses (an old field name, a city ID that was split). The session ID would make the cache nearly useless, since the parse does not depend on who asked.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
question: At k=100, L=100, w=20, FIRST brings our modeled query latency from 10.35 s to 2.39 s. Which next change cuts FIRST's latency the most?
options: Raising the window step s while keeping w = 20, which removes windows and their prefill
Asking for a shorter permutation format
Using a higher sampling temperature
Adding a reasoning step before the ranking
explain: FIRST has no permutation to shorten, so the remaining time is prefill on a chain of windows. Fewer windows (or fewer tokens per window) is what is left. A reasoning step would add decode tokens back.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
question: Your API returns only generated text, no log-probabilities. Which pointwise method can you still run, and with what limitation?
options: Query likelihood, because it uses teacher forcing
Neither; pointwise prompts cannot work without fine-tuning
Yes/No generation, but you only get a binary label, so many passages tie and the ranking is coarse
Both, as long as you set temperature to 0
explain: Query likelihood needs the probability of the given query tokens, which a text-only API cannot provide. Yes/No still produces an answer, but without p(Yes) you only get two buckets, so passages inside a bucket keep their original order.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers
question: Your listwise reranker works well on BM25 input but degrades badly when you switch the first stage to a new retriever that returns candidates in a near-random order. Which fix targets the cause?
options: Increase the window step so fewer windows are needed
Lower the temperature to 0
Shuffle the input several times and aggregate the rankings, or use a student trained with shuffled inputs
Switch to query likelihood, which is order-free but needs no changes
explain: The symptom is order sensitivity: failures and the one-pass guarantee both lean on a good initial order. Permutation self-consistency marginalizes the order out, and RankVicuna/RankZephyr train on shuffled inputs for the same reason. Temperature 0 makes outputs repeatable, not order-invariant.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Evaluating routers: cost-quality curves, PGR, APGR and CPT
question: A router has r = 7.6 on a benchmark where the weak model scores 6.5 and the strong model 8.4. What is its PGR?
explain: PGR = (7.6 - 6.5) / (8.4 - 6.5) = 1.1 / 1.9 = 0.579. 0.905 is 7.6 / 8.4, which ignores the weak baseline; 0.421 is 1 minus the right answer.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Matching descriptors and Lowe's ratio test
question: You lower the ratio threshold from 0.8 to 0.6. What happens?
options: More matches survive and the outlier fraction rises
Nothing, since the ratio is scale-free
Every correct match is kept and only outliers are removed
Fewer matches survive and the surviving set has a lower outlier fraction
explain: A lower threshold demands a clearer winner, so fewer matches pass. Those that pass are less likely to be wrong, but some correct matches are lost too. Lowe's 0.8 removed 90% of false matches while losing under 5% of correct ones on the test data.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
question: A team uses 64-bit node indices plus a 16-bit tag packed into a 128-bit word and CASes it with a double-word CAS. Their threads can be descheduled for seconds. What is the honest risk statement?
options: ABA is impossible with any tag
ABA becomes very unlikely but not impossible: the 16-bit tag wraps after 65,536 successful CASes on that word
ABA is only possible on ARM
The tag makes the algorithm wait-free
explain: Michael and Scott: counters make ABA extremely unlikely but do not guarantee it never happens. At high CAS rates a 16-bit tag wraps in milliseconds, so a long stall gives many chances. With a 128-bit word there is room for a much wider tag, which is the cheap fix.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
question: Your service emits 50 GB of logs per hour and you must assign a template to every line as it arrives. Which property of a parser matters most for that?
options: It must achieve the highest possible accuracy on a labelled benchmark, whatever the cost
It must be online: constant work per line, no pass over the whole log before the first answer
It must store every raw line so templates can be recomputed later
It must know the number of distinct templates in advance to size its data structures
explain: At 33,000 to 56,000 lines per second you need bounded per-line work and no training pass. Offline parsers such as LKE are quadratic in the line count and could not finish four of five datasets in the Drain evaluation. Template counts are not knowable in advance, which is the whole problem, and retaining raw lines is a storage decision, not a parsing one.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
question: You cap Drain3 at max_clusters = 5000 with LRU eviction, and persist nothing. You restart the service. What breaks?
options: Nothing: the tree is rebuilt from the stream within a few seconds
Only the counts for templates that had been evicted before the restart
Parsing accuracy, because the LRU cache warms up in a different order
Every template id is reassigned from scratch, so every stored series, dashboard and trained model keyed on those ids silently refers to the wrong template
explain: Template ids are assigned by an incrementing counter as clusters are created. Without a persisted snapshot a restart renumbers everything in whatever order the stream happens to arrive, so id 7 now means something else. Drain3 exists partly to solve this: it snapshots state to a file, Redis or Kafka and reloads on startup. Accuracy itself recovers quickly; identity does not.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Normalisation: one event, one shape (ECS and OCSF)
question: Why keep the raw text in event.original after normalising?
options: Schemas forbid deleting fields
ECS requires it for authentication events
It makes queries faster
It lets you re-parse old events after fixing a mapping bug and shows exactly what the source said
explain: Normalised fields are an interpretation. When an interpretation turns out wrong, the original is the only way to recover the truth for past events.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The detection lifecycle: hypothesis to retirement
question: Which ADS section would have warned the team that the MFA device rule gets noisy when a popular phone launches?
options: Goal
Priority
Categorization
False Positives
explain: Known benign triggers belong in False Positives, together with how to tell them apart. FireEye's 2020 detection (lesson 16) came from exactly such an alert, investigated despite that known noise.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Tuning and allowlisting without blinding yourself
question: Which allowlist is safest for a deployment agent that triggers the PowerShell rule?
options: CommandLine contains 'DeployAgent'
Exact ParentImage path under Program Files, plus the signer and the managed-host group
ParentImage endswith `\DeployAgent.exe`
Any event from user svc_deploy
explain: Only the exact-path option uses facts an attacker cannot cheaply forge: a path standard users cannot write to, a code-signing identity, and an inventory-defined scope. The others can be met by renaming a file, adding a word, or stealing one account.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Proving it works: purple teams, emulation and metrics
question: Incident detection times this quarter were 2, 4, 6, 8 and 700 hours. Which statement is accurate?
options: The median is 6 hours; the 700-hour incident should be examined on its own
The mean, 144 hours, describes a typical incident
The median is 144 hours
Both mean and median are 6 hours
explain: Mean = 720 / 5 = 144 hours, pulled up by one case; median = 6 hours. Report both and investigate the outlier.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
question: A Llama 3 8B deployment wants to prefill 128K-token prompts. Roughly what share of the prefill FLOPs is attention rather than weight matrix multiplies?
options: About 5%: weights always dominate
Exactly 50%, by symmetry
About 70%
About 99%
explain: Weights: 2N x n = 15.0 GFLOP x 131,072 = 1.97 PFLOP. Attention: 2 x 32 x 4096 x 131,072 squared = 4.50 PFLOP. Attention is 4.50 / 6.47 = 70%. The share keeps rising with length: 36% at 32K, 95% at 1M.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Universal Transformers: recurrence over depth with a halting rule
question: A position's halting unit outputs 0.3, 0.5, 0.4 at steps 1 to 3, with epsilon = 0.01. When does it halt and what is its remainder?
options: Step 2, remainder 0.2
Step 3, remainder 0.2
Step 3, remainder 0.4
It never halts because the sum never equals exactly 0.99
explain: Running sums are 0.3, 0.8, 1.2. The first to reach 0.99 is step 3, so N = 3. The remainder is 1 minus the sum before the halting step: 1 - 0.8 = 0.2. The step-3 halting probability (0.4) is replaced by the remainder so the weights sum to 1.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Build it: loop your GPT with input injection and random depth
question: During training your recurrent-depth model logs validation loss 0.81 at r = 1 and 0.80 at r = 32, and the gap has not grown for thousands of steps; mean cosine similarity between states is a steady 0.3. What is the most likely problem?
options: The learning rate is too low, so both losses fall slowly
Representation collapse: all token states have become identical
The model has learned to ignore its recurrent state, so extra iterations do nothing
Nothing; equal losses mean the loop has converged
explain: Equal loss at 1 and 32 iterations means the core's output does not depend on how many times it ran: the model solved what it could without the loop. That was Huginn's second failed run and our step-signal variant. Collapse shows up in the cosine-similarity monitor instead; converged loops still differ sharply between r = 1 and r = 32.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
question: You fine-tune a 7B model with Adam but freeze all but 1% of its weights. Which part of the 107.8 GB shrinks the most?
options: The 16-bit copy of the frozen weights, because frozen weights are not loaded
Nothing changes, because Adam allocates state for every weight in the model
Gradients and Adam states, because they are only needed for trainable weights
Activations, because a frozen layer does not store activations
explain: Frozen weights still have to sit in memory for the forward pass, and activations are still needed to backpropagate into trainable parts. But gradients and the three fp32 optimizer tensors exist only for trainable parameters, so 14 of the 16 bytes per parameter disappear for the frozen 99%.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: QLoRA: fine-tuning on top of a 4-bit base model
question: Why does NF4 put more of its 16 levels near zero than a uniform 4-bit integer grid does?
options: Because pretrained weights are roughly normal, so equal-probability bins are dense where most weights lie
Because zero-valued weights are pruned and need no levels
Because the GPU can only multiply by values close to zero
Because the adapters only change weights near zero
explain: NF4 is a quantile quantizer for a normal distribution: each of the 16 bins holds about the same share of weights. Since most weights cluster near zero, the levels cluster there too, which lowers average rounding error for normally distributed data.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Composing adapters: switching, merging and task arithmetic
question: DARE drops 90% of an adapter's delta entries (p = 0.9). By what factor must the surviving entries be multiplied so each output keeps its expected value?
options: No rescaling is needed: the dropped entries average out
explain: The factor is 1/(1 - p) = 1/0.1 = 10. Each entry survives with probability 0.1, so ten times its value in expectation gives back the original. The DARE paper reports that dropping 30 to 40% without rescaling already hurt results noticeably.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
question: RMU drops Zephyr-7B's WMDP-Bio accuracy from 63.7% to 31.2% while overall MMLU moves from 58.1% to 57.1%. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The hazardous knowledge has been erased from the weights
RMU has no side effects
The model no longer answers the proxy questions, with little general cost but real loss in nearby topics like virology
WMDP-Bio is now harder than random guessing
explain: Multiple-choice accuracy near 25% means the model no longer selects the right answers. The table also shows MMLU virology falling from 52.4% to 25.9%, so related benign knowledge was hit. Whether the knowledge is still in the weights is a separate question that fine-tuning attacks answer (Lesson 6).

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: How a Mac defends itself: the layers from boot to app
question: A user pastes a command from a web page into Terminal, and it downloads and runs a shell script. Which layer from Apple's three-layer model was designed to stop this first step?
options: Prevent launch: Gatekeeper and notarization check the script before it runs
SIP, because the script runs as the user
TCC, because Terminal is a protected app
None of them directly: the three layers are built around apps and files, so a typed command skips the launch checks
explain: Gatekeeper and notarization evaluate apps and files that arrive with quarantine. A command typed by the user is the user acting. Later layers (XProtect behaviour rules, TCC, logging) may still catch what the script does, which is why defenders need more than launch checks.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: XProtect: Apple's built-in signatures and remediators
question: A new Shlayer variant is rebuilt with a different hash every hour. Which built-in control is best placed to catch it without Apple seeing each copy?
options: An XProtect YARA rule matching patterns shared by the family
A notarization revocation ticket
SIP
The quarantine attribute
explain: Revocations and hashes name specific files. A YARA rule describes patterns common to the family, so new builds still match. Apple's guide makes exactly this contrast.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Hardened runtime, library validation and dylib injection
question: An attacker sets `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` in a LaunchAgent that starts a notarized app which holds Full Disk Access. Assuming no exception entitlements, what happens?
options: The library loads and inherits Full Disk Access
Gatekeeper blocks the LaunchAgent
SIP deletes the library
dyld ignores the variable because notarized apps run with the hardened runtime
explain: Notarization requires the hardened runtime, under which DYLD environment variables are ignored unless the app has the allow-dyld-environment-variables entitlement. That is exactly why that entitlement is worth inventorying.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Hunting across a fleet: osquery tables and detection logic
question: Your EDR shows `/usr/bin/dscl . -authonly ana` whose grandparent is `osascript`, launched from Terminal two seconds after a paste. What is the best reading?
options: Routine directory lookup
Likely a script validating a password the user just typed into a fake prompt: escalate
A macOS update
Harmless because dscl is Apple-signed
explain: Microsoft observed stealers validating captured passwords with dscl -authonly. Apple-signed tools used in an attacker's sequence are living-off-the-land (abusing tools already on the system); the ancestry is what makes it suspicious.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Case: 3CX, a notarized app with a poisoned library
question: Why did library validation not stop the malicious libffmpeg.dylib?
options: Library validation is off for Electron apps
The dylib was loaded by Gatekeeper
SIP was disabled on customer Macs
The dylib was signed as part of 3CX's own build with the same Team ID as the app
explain: Library validation refuses libraries from other teams. A compromised build pipeline signs the malicious library with the vendor's own identity, so the check passes.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: A safe analysis lab and the analysis workflow
question: Why use a simulated internet (INetSim, FakeNet-NG) instead of no network at all?
options: It makes the malware run faster
It is required by law
The sample often reveals its domains and protocols only when something answers, and nothing real is reached
It hides the analysis VM from the malware
explain: With no network, many samples stall at their first lookup. A fake service answers, so you capture the domains, URLs and protocol the sample uses, while nothing leaves the lab.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Disassemblers and decompilers: from bytes back to C
question: A decompiler shows `if (local_14 < 0x5a)` but you suspect a signed versus unsigned mistake matters for a size check. What should you do?
options: Trust the decompiler; it is always exact
Rename local_14 and move on
Check the conditional jump in the disassembly: jl or jg mean signed, jb or ja mean unsigned
Rerun the decompiler with a different font
explain: The jump instruction is the ground truth for signedness. Decompilers guess types; when the detail matters, confirm in assembly.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Writing and testing YARA rules
question: Why did notes.txt not match, even though it contains both the banner and the URL?
options: YARA cannot read .txt files
The condition requires uint16(0) == 0x5A4D, and the text file does not start with MZ
The filesize was too large
nocase only works on PE files
explain: The condition combines file structure and content. A text file that quotes the strings fails the structural check, which is exactly the false positive the check was added to prevent.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: How rankings shift as you cut dimensions: Matryoshka vs standard
question: With a Matryoshka model you shortlist with 2-d prefixes and keep the top 3 documents. In the toy, which statement is true?
options: The shortlist is B, A, C, so the true best match A survives, and the 8-d rerank puts A first
The shortlist is A, B, C in exact final order, so no rerank is needed
The shortlist is C, B, A, so A is lost
A 2-d prefix cannot be used for search at all
explain: At m = 2 the Matryoshka scores are B 1.000, A 1.000, C 0.998: the right documents, in blurred order. Reranking those three at m = 8 gives A 0.997, B 0.757, C 0.616. A shortlist needs to contain the right items, not order them perfectly.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
question: p = 8 pipeline stages, m = 32 microbatches, interleaved with v = 4 chunks per device. What is the bubble as a fraction of ideal time?
explain: (p - 1) / (v m) = 7 / (4 x 32) = 7/128 = 5.5%. Without interleaving it would be 7/32 = 21.9%.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Mixture of experts at scale: EP, token dispatch and parallel folding
question: A team moves an MoE model from EP = 8 inside one 8-GPU server to EP = 16 across two servers, keeping everything else the same. Which part of the step grows most, and why?
options: The expert GEMMs, because each GPU now holds twice as many experts
The router, because it must score twice as many experts
The dispatch and combine all-to-alls, because about half of each token's expert copies now cross the slower inter-node network
Nothing, the all-to-all volume per GPU is unchanged
explain: With 16 ranks over 2 servers, about 8/16 of a token's experts live on the other server, so roughly half the dispatch and combine bytes leave NVLink for the network, which is many times slower. Each GPU holds fewer experts, not more. This is why the guide keeps EP x TP inside the NVLink domain and uses PP across nodes.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: What only RAM knows: Duqu 2.0 and the case for memory
question: Kaspersky advised rebooting every computer in the network at the same moment to remove Duqu 2.0. Why at the same moment?
options: Because Windows updates install only during a simultaneous reboot
Because the malware's files on disk are deleted only on a cold boot
Because the malware lived only in memory and re-infected cleaned machines from infected ones, so a staggered reboot lets it spread back
Because rebooting one at a time corrupts the domain controller
explain: Duqu 2.0 had no persistence and survived by re-infecting rebooted machines from those still infected. Rebooting everything at once removes every in-memory copy together. It had no files to delete.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Inside Volatility 3: layers, symbols, templates and automagic
question: A Linux image analysis fails with no symbol table found. You have an ISF built from the same distribution's kernel version 5.15.0-91, but the image's banner shows a different build date. What should you do?
options: Rename the existing ISF so its banner matches
Use the ISF anyway; same version number means same layout
Find the debug kernel that matches the banner exactly and build its ISF with dwarf2json
Switch to the Windows plugins
explain: Volatility requires an exact banner match because structure layouts change with configuration and build. Forcing a near match produces plausible-looking wrong answers.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Hollowing, reflective loading and how memory gives them away
question: hollowprocesses reports that a process's PEB ImageBaseAddress differs from its EPROCESS SectionBaseAddress. Why is that meaningful?
options: The PEB is writable by code in the process while the section base is kept in kernel memory, so a mismatch suggests the image was replaced and the PEB edited
It means the process is 32-bit on a 64-bit system
It shows the image file was deleted from disk
It is normal for every service
explain: The two values normally agree. Hollowing techniques often rewrite the user-side PEB to cover the swap, which the kernel-side value does not follow.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Linux memory: banners, task lists, bash history and kernel checks
question: The banners plugin shows two different kernel versions in one image. Which one must your ISF match?
options: The first one printed
The banner of the kernel that was actually running, which you confirm from collection notes such as uname -a
The oldest one
Either; Volatility merges them
explain: Old banners can survive in memory from earlier kernels or cached files. Volatility needs the exact running kernel's banner, so record uname -a when you collect.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
question: A service's allocator reports 2.0 GiB allocated to the application at every sample for a week, while resident memory rises from 2.4 GiB to 3.6 GiB. What is the best first hypothesis?
options: Fragmentation: the gap between held and live memory is growing
A memory leak in the application
The kernel is counting page cache as resident
Internal fragmentation from size classes, which grows over time
explain: Allocated bytes are flat, so live data is not growing: that rules out a leak. The growing gap is memory the allocator holds but cannot reuse or return. Size-class rounding is fixed per object, so it cannot grow while the same objects stay live.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Measuring and fixing fragmentation in production
question: Why can Mesh return memory from a C++ program without updating any pointers?
options: It copies objects to new addresses and patches pointers found by scanning the stack
It only frees pages that have no live objects
It merges two physical pages whose live objects sit at different offsets and maps both virtual pages to one
It relies on the kernel's compaction to move pages
explain: Objects keep their virtual addresses and offsets. Only the virtual-to-physical mapping changes: two virtual pages share one physical page whose slots now hold both sets of objects. Scanning for pointers is impossible in C/C++ because pointers can be hidden or disguised.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: SeqCst, fences, and when you need one global order
question: You replace `X.store(1, SeqCst)` with `fence(SeqCst); X.store(1, Relaxed)`. Is that equivalent?
options: Yes, a SeqCst fence plus a Relaxed store is exactly a SeqCst store
Yes, but only on x86
No: the fence is in the SeqCst total order but the store is not, so other SeqCst operations need not agree on where the store sits
No: fences can only be used with loads
explain: Mara Bos notes this explicitly: only the fence takes part in the single total order, not the atomic operations around it, so a SeqCst operation cannot be split into a relaxed operation and a fence. Release and Acquire can be split that way; SeqCst cannot.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
question: Thread T is pinned in epoch 5 and stays pinned. What is the highest value the global epoch can reach?
options: Unbounded, since other threads keep advancing
explain: Advancing from 5 to 6 is allowed because T is pinned in 5, the current epoch. Advancing from 6 to 7 requires every pinned thread to be in 6, and T is still in 5. So the epoch stops at 6, and garbage tagged 5 or later (freeable at 7 or later) piles up.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
question: Which outcome of an out-of-bounds write is usually hardest to notice?
options: A crash with a segmentation fault
A compiler error
A neighbouring variable silently changes and the program keeps running
The operating system logs the write
explain: A crash is loud and gets reported. A quiet change to a neighbour, such as a permission flag or a length, produces wrong behaviour with no error at all. The compiler accepts the code, and the operating system only notices accesses to unmapped memory.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Out-of-bounds reads: Heartbleed and why leaks matter
question: In the vulnerable echo, which single value should have limited the copy?
options: claimed, the length field from the message
rec_len, the number of bytes actually received
sizeof out
The constant 64
explain: claimed is what the sender says; rec_len is what really arrived. The copy must not read beyond rec_len. (Checking against sizeof out as well protects the destination, but would not have stopped the leak.)

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Format string bugs: when user text becomes instructions
question: Which call is safe when `msg` comes from a network client?
options: printf(msg);
syslog(LOG_INFO, msg);
fprintf(stderr, "%s", msg);
sprintf(out, msg);
explain: Only fprintf with a literal "%s" keeps msg as data. syslog and sprintf take a format string as well, so passing msg there has the same bug as printf(msg).

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
question: Anchor-positive distance is 0.40 and margin is 0.2. A negative sits at 0.50. Which band is it in and what is the loss?
options: Semi-hard, loss 0.10
Easy, loss 0
Hard, loss 0.30
Semi-hard, loss 0.30
explain: 0.40 < 0.50 < 0.60, so the negative is further than the positive but inside the margin: semi-hard. Loss = 0.40 - 0.50 + 0.2 = 0.10.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: When the optimizer deletes the code you meant to time
question: Which change alone stops clang from folding `bench_fold` into one multiply?
options: Returning s from the function
Marking compute as inline
Passing the input as a function parameter whose value the compiler cannot see, instead of the literal 42
Increasing n to 10 billion
explain: bench_fold already returns s, and that did not help: folding needs only that the input be known. An inline hint changes nothing (compute was already inlined). A larger n changes the multiply, not the strategy. An unknown input stops the folding, but clang still runs compute once before the loop and multiplies by n (hoisting, next lesson).

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
question: You need to post-train a 700B-parameter MoE whose training job spans several racks and needs expert parallelism. Which training backend do the Miles docs point you to?
options: Megatron-LM, the default and the backend for 100B+ MoE models that need model parallelism
FSDP, because it loads the Hugging Face checkpoint with no conversion
torchtitan, because it is driven as a black box
Any of them; the backend only changes checkpoint format
explain: The training-backend page says to use Megatron-LM for large models and anything that needs real parallelism, such as a 100B+ MoE or a job spanning racks. FSDP is the fast path for new architectures and models that fit under data parallelism alone. The backend changes how the model is split, not only its checkpoints.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Connecting an environment: rollout, generate and agent functions
question: You replace Miles's rollout function with the Verifiers connector. What do you give up, and what stays in Miles?
options: Nothing changes except the reward function
You lose the trainer's advantage computation but keep TITO recording
You lose weight updates to the engines, which Verifiers now owns
You keep Miles's data source but lose batching
You lose Miles's session-server token recording, its data source and its batch orchestration including group filtering; engines, weight updates, advantages and optimizer stay
explain: The rollout function is the outermost layer, so a connector there takes over the agent loop, recording, rewards, the taskset and grouping and filtering. The environments table marks the model, engines, weight updates, advantages and optimizer as staying in Miles for every connector.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: LoRA RL and the multi-LoRA training service
question: A colleague launches a multi-LoRA gateway with --colocate to save GPUs, and separately asks for P2P transfer in a single-LoRA disaggregated run. What happens?
options: Both work; LoRA sync is transport-agnostic
Multi-LoRA works colocated, but P2P is rejected
Both are rejected only on AMD GPUs
Multi-LoRA rejects --colocate because adapter gradients stay in GPU buffers between calls, and single-LoRA sync uses NCCL broadcast since P2P and disk-delta do not carry adapters
explain: The multi-LoRA page lists separate training and sampling GPUs as a hard constraint (no --colocate, no --offload-train). The LoRA page says the P2P/RDMA and disk-delta modes do not support LoRA; disaggregated single-LoRA uses --update-weight-transfer-mode broadcast.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
question: Which statement about learned indexes, LRB and Decima is correct?
options: All three need the model to be correct to return correct results
None of them needs retraining once deployed
In all three, the model chooses among options the system already guarantees are valid, so mistakes cost performance rather than correctness
All three use deep neural networks at decision time
explain: The index searches a verified window (or a B-tree leaf), LRB evicts some cached object, and Decima only schedules runnable stages. Model quality changes speed or miss ratio. LRB uses GBMs and the index uses mostly linear leaves, and both indexes and caches need retraining as data changes.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Dynamic analysis: a test device, a proxy and the app's own files
question: You install Burp's CA certificate in the user store of a lab phone and set the Wi-Fi proxy. A browser's traffic appears in Burp, but the shopping app (release build, targets API 34, no network security config) shows only failed handshakes. What does this tell you?
options: The app is pinning certificates, which is a vulnerability
Burp is misconfigured, because the browser would fail too
The app is using the platform default for apps targeting Android 7.0 and later: it trusts only system CAs, which is correct behaviour
The app does not use HTTPS
explain: Since API level 24, apps trust only the system store unless their network security config says otherwise; with no config they use that safe default. The browser trusts user CAs, so it works. Failed handshakes show TLS is in use and validated. Use a debug build or a system-store CA on a rooted lab device.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Deep links: custom schemes, App Links and Universal Links
question: Why does RFC 8252 forbid using an in-app WebView for the OAuth login page?
options: WebViews cannot display HTTPS pages
WebViews do not support JavaScript
The app hosting the WebView can read what the user types and the cookies, so a malicious or compromised app could capture the user's credentials for the identity provider
Identity providers block WebView user agents by law
explain: In an embedded user-agent the host app controls the page and can inspect it, which defeats the point of OAuth (the app should never see the password). The system browser or an in-app browser tab keeps the identity provider's page out of the app's reach.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Resilience and attestation: what an app can prove, and what it cannot
question: In the assertion model, why must the server check that the counter increases, when the signature already proves the request came from the attested key?
options: Because signatures can be forged when the counter is low
Because the counter encrypts the request
Because Apple requires a counter on every HTTP request
Because a captured, validly signed request could otherwise be replayed as-is; the counter and the one-time challenge make each assertion usable once
explain: A signature says who signed, not how many times the bytes may be used. Our run shows the replay passing the signature check but failing the counter check. Apple's server-side steps include both the counter comparison and matching the one-time challenge.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Absorbing the up-projections: attend in latent space
question: Which property of matrix multiplication makes absorbing $W^{UK}$ into the query legal?
options: Commutativity: $AB = BA$
Associativity: $(AB)C = A(BC)$, so the up-projection can be grouped with the query instead of the latent
Distributivity over the softmax
Invertibility of $W^{UK}$
explain: Only regrouping is needed. Matrix products are not commutative in general, and $W^{UK}$ is not square (it maps 512 to 128 x 128), so it is not invertible. Lesson 4 shows how RoPE breaks this regrouping.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, FP8 cache
question: FlashMLA's FP8 cache for DeepSeek-V3.2 quantizes the 512 latent values but keeps the 64 RoPE values in BF16. Which statement is right?
options: The RoPE part must be BF16 because FP8 cannot represent rotations
The README gives accuracy as the reason, and it costs little: 128 of the 656 bytes
The RoPE part is kept in BF16 because it is shared by all heads and so is never read
FP8 with scale stores the whole row, RoPE included, in E4M3
explain: The README states the RoPE part "is not quantized for accuracy". Rotation math works on any number format, and the RoPE key is read for every score. Keeping it in BF16 adds 64 bytes per row compared with quantizing it too.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
question: A team serves a 4-bit base with one hot QLoRA-trained adapter. To remove the LoRA overhead they merge the adapter into the 4-bit weights and quantize the result again. What is the likely outcome?
options: Nothing changes: merging is exact in any number format
The merged model loses much of the fine-tune, because requantizing rounds away most of the small update
The KV cache must be recomputed in 4 bits, which slows decode
vLLM refuses to serve a base that was ever merged
explain: A 4-bit step is coarse compared with a LoRA update, so the round trip turns most of BA into rounding noise. Keep the adapter unmerged in 16 bits beside the quantized base, or merge into a dequantized 16-bit copy and accept its memory cost.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Multi-LoRA in vLLM and LoRAX, and the cost model
question: Traffic is 95% for one adapter, with a long tail of 300 rarely used adapters. Which design fits best?
options: A multi-LoRA server that keeps the hot adapter resident and loads tail adapters on demand from CPU memory
Merge all 300 into separate model copies
Merge-and-swap on a single GPU for all traffic
Serve only the base model
explain: The tail is what makes separate or swapped deployments expensive. A multi-LoRA server batches everything over one base, keeps the popular adapter in GPU memory, and fetches rare ones on demand. A dedicated merged copy for the hot adapter can still make sense if its latency is critical.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
question: In the toy, why does d2 (not relevant) outrank d7 (relevant) after fusing all four lists?
options: d2 has a higher cosine similarity
d2 appears in two lists while d7 appears in only one, and RRF sums contributions
RRF gives rank 1 a weight of zero
d7 was removed by deduplication
explain: RRF adds one term per list. d2 gets 1/62 + 1/65 = 0.03151; d7 gets only 1/61 = 0.01639 even though it was ranked first by q2. Agreement beats a single strong vote.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Candidate depth k and the recall ceiling
question: Your RAG search uses BM25 top 100 and a strong cross-encoder. You swap in a cross-encoder twice as large and nDCG@10 barely moves. Stage 1 recall@100 is 0.62. What is the most likely bottleneck?
options: The new cross-encoder is undertrained
The ceiling: 38% of relevant documents never reach the reranker, so stage 1 recall or k must improve
nDCG@10 cannot measure reranker quality
k = 100 is too deep and confuses the reranker
explain: With recall@100 of 0.62, the reranker never sees 38% of relevant documents. Bigger rerankers only reorder the 62% they receive. Raise the ceiling: hybrid first stage, better embeddings, or a larger k if the budget allows.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
question: A 10-token sequence is trained with n = 4 independent future heads. How many loss terms does it contribute (count head i as having 10 - i targets)?
options: 9, because only the next-token head counts
40, because each of 10 positions has 4 targets
36, because 4 x 9
explain: Head 1 has targets for positions 1 to 9, head 2 for positions 1 to 8, and so on: 9 + 8 + 7 + 6 = 30. Positions near the end have fewer valid future tokens, so the count is not simply 10 x 4.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Add MTP to your GPT: both designs in about 60 lines
question: A colleague's MTP model trains fine, but its head-2 loss tracks the head-1 loss almost exactly from the first step. They compute head 2's loss as cross_entropy(logits2[:, :-2], x[:, 1:-1]). What is wrong?
options: Nothing; head 2 is expected to match head 1
logits2 should be sliced [:, 2:] instead of [:, :-2]
cross_entropy needs the targets one-hot encoded
The targets are shifted by 1 instead of 2, so head 2 is learning the next token again
explain: Position t must be paired with x[t+2]: logits2[:, :-2] with x[:, 2:]. With x[:, 1:-1] the shapes still match, so nothing crashes, but every pair is (position t, token t+1), the next-token task. Slicing the logits [:, 2:] would pair later positions with earlier tokens.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why a weight matrix is not a bag of independent numbers
question: You need $H^{-1/2}$ for $H = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ (eigenvalues 3 and 1). A colleague computes it by raising each entry to the power $-1/2$. Why is that wrong?
options: It is right, because H is symmetric, so entry and matrix powers agree
It is wrong only for matrices with negative entries; for this H it gives the same answer
A matrix power acts on eigen-directions, Q Lambda^(-1/2) Q-transpose; the entrywise result does not satisfy X H X = I
It is wrong because inverse roots only exist for diagonal matrices
explain: The matrix power is $Q\Lambda^{-1/2}Q^\top$, here $\frac12\begin{bmatrix}1+3^{-1/2} & 3^{-1/2}-1\\ 3^{-1/2}-1 & 1+3^{-1/2}\end{bmatrix} \approx \begin{bmatrix}0.789&-0.211\\-0.211&0.789\end{bmatrix}$. The entrywise version gives $\begin{bmatrix}0.707&1\\1&0.707\end{bmatrix}$, which is not even close, and with negative entries it is undefined.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
question: Why does SOAP lose less than Shampoo when eigenvectors are recomputed only every 100 steps?
options: SOAP uses a more accurate eigensolver than Shampoo
SOAP keeps updating Adam's second moment every step in the slowly changing basis, while Shampoo's preconditioner is frozen between refreshes
SOAP does not use L and R at all
SOAP uses a larger learning rate that hides the staleness
explain: Both compute their expensive rotation or roots rarely. Between refreshes Shampoo applies a fixed preconditioner (grafting adapts only a scalar per layer), whereas SOAP's $V$ keeps tracking per-coordinate scale. The paper's explanation is exactly this continual second-moment update in the current basis.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
question: Which comparison gives the most trustworthy estimate of an optimizer's speedup over AdamW?
options: The new optimizer with a swept learning rate against AdamW with the learning rate from the GPT-3 recipe
Both optimizers with the same fixed learning rate and weight decay, to keep the comparison controlled
A single 1.2B run with each optimizer's default settings
Each optimizer tuned separately, at several model sizes and data ratios, compared at the end of training
explain: Shared hyperparameters are not neutral: Lion's best weight decay is about 0.6 versus AdamW's 0.1, so fixing them favors one side. An untuned baseline can inflate a gain by up to 2x. A single run at one scale says little about others.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Deriving the rules from one condition, and muP by hand
question: You add a new input layer: a learned embedding whose fan_in is the vocabulary size $V$ (finite) and whose fan_out is $d_{model}$ (grows with width). You train with Adam. How should its learning rate scale as $d_{model}$ grows?
options: Like $1/d_{model}$, as for hidden weights
Like $1/\sqrt{d_{model}}$
Constant in width: Adam LR is $1/\text{fan\_in} = 1/V$, and $V$ does not grow
Like $d_{model}$, as SGD would
explain: With Adam the spectral condition gives $\eta \propto 1/\text{fan\_in}$ for every layer. The fan_in here is the vocabulary, which is finite, so the LR is constant in width, matching the input-weights column of Table 3. (For one-hot inputs the paper also replaces the input length $\sqrt{V}$ by 1, which changes constants, not the width scaling.) Under SGD the answer would instead grow like fan_out.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Transferring across depth: branch multipliers, Depth-muP, CompleteP
question: Why does Tensor Programs VI say its $1/\sqrt{L}$ rule is no longer optimal for Transformers?
options: Transformers use LayerNorm
Attention is not a residual branch
Transformers are trained with Adam rather than SGD
Each Transformer block contains two or more layers, and with block depth 2 or more the layers inside a block interact additively, hurting performance and shifting the optimum
explain: The theory is clean for blocks with one layer. With block depth 2 or more, keeping feature diversity forces the layers within a block to interact additively instead of multiplicatively, so performance drops and HPs shift with depth (Section 9 of the paper). CompleteP's $\alpha = 1$ is one response to this.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
question: Why does FUTEX_WAIT take an expected value at all, instead of simply sleeping?
options: To pick which waiter FUTEX_WAKE will wake
To set the futex word to that value before sleeping
So a wake-up that happened after the caller's check but before it was queued is not lost
So the kernel can store the lock state between calls
explain: The waiter decided to sleep based on an earlier load. If an unlock and wake happened after that load, the word has changed, and the atomic compare in FUTEX_WAIT catches it. The kernel never stores the lock state; it just compares.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
question: A Repeatable Read transaction only runs plain SELECT statements (no FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE). Can it fail with a serialization error in PostgreSQL?
options: Yes, whenever another transaction updates a row it read
No, the docs say read-only Repeatable Read transactions never have serialization conflicts
Yes, if it reads more than one table
Only if it runs longer than the statement timeout
explain: The 40001 at Repeatable Read comes from trying to modify or lock a row changed after the snapshot. A transaction that only reads never does that, so it never needs a retry at this level.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The task: pull typed spans out of running text
question: What does the reduction to per-token labelling buy you?
options: It removes the need for a decoder, since the labels are already the spans
It lets the model predict overlapping entities
It guarantees the predicted spans are always valid
It turns an unbounded structured output into one fixed-size classification per position, which any classifier can emit
explain: One label per token is a fixed-size decision per position, which any classifier can emit. You still need a decoder, the output can still be an invalid tag sequence, and a single chain of labels cannot represent overlapping spans at all.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Transformer taggers and subword alignment
question: In the Hugging Face recipe, why do continuation sub-pieces get -100 rather than the word's label?
options: Because -100 is a reserved label id for the O class
Because the loss would otherwise be dominated by long words
Because the tokenizer cannot tell which word a continuation piece belongs to
Because the classifier is trained and read out on the first piece of each word, so the other pieces must be excluded from the loss
explain: -100 is the ignore index of PyTorch's cross-entropy, not a class. The convention is one prediction per word, taken at the word's first piece, exactly as the BERT paper describes, so every other piece must be masked out of the loss.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Doctrine in public: persistent engagement and responsible cyber power
question: A blog post says 'China's military doctrine requires pre-positioning in US water utilities'. What should a careful analyst do with this sentence?
options: Repeat it as fact, since US agencies have said similar things
Drop it, since doctrine is never relevant to defence
Replace 'requires' with 'may require' and keep it unsourced
Check whether it quotes a primary Chinese text or another government's assessment, and label it accordingly in any brief
explain: The US assessment about Chinese actors' behaviour is real and citable, but it is an assessment by another government, not Chinese doctrine. Keep provenance visible; hedging words do not fix a missing source.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Responses: naming, indictments, sanctions and disruption
question: What did the December 2023 KV Botnet operation do, according to DOJ?
options: Permanently patched every infected router
Arrested the Volt Typhoon operators in China
Deleted the malware from infected US routers and blocked their links to the botnet; the blocking steps were temporary, and a restart would undo them
Took control of the routers' owners' networks to monitor them
explain: DOJ says the court-authorised steps deleted the malware and severed connections, did not collect content, and are temporary; owners were told to replace end-of-life routers. No arrests or patches are described.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: North Korea's revenue operations: banks, crypto and IT workers
question: The Bangladesh Bank operators attempted to move USD 851 million but stole USD 81 million. According to Treasury, what stopped the rest?
options: SWIFT's software rejected messages over a fixed limit
The bank's antivirus detected the malware during the transfers
The Federal Reserve required two-factor approval for every transfer
A typographical error alerted personnel, who then prevented the additional transfers
explain: Treasury: the operators made over 36 large transfer requests 'before a typographical error alerted personnel'. The sources describe no automatic limit, antivirus detection or extra approval step stopping the transfers.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
question: With NSA's settings ($d=16$, $n=16$, $l'=64$, $w=512$), which term of the per-query key count dominates at a 1M-token context?
options: The compressed tokens, about $t/d \approx 65{,}500$
The selected tokens, $nl' = 1024$
The window, $w = 512$
All three are equal
explain: Selection and window are fixed sizes. Compression grows linearly with $t$ at rate $1/d$, so at long context it dominates: about 65,534 of roughly 67,070 keys at 1,048,576 tokens.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Write NSA and DSA as masked attention and test them against dense
question: Why does `cmp_mask` compare the query position with the last token of each compression block, not the first?
options: Because the last token always has the largest key
To make the compressed keys differentiable
It is arbitrary; either choice gives a valid causal model
Because a summary mixes all l tokens of its block, so using it before the block ends would leak future tokens into the past
explain: The MLP reads the whole block, so its output depends on every token in it. A query that saw the summary before the block ended would get information from tokens after itself, which breaks causal training and cannot be reproduced at decode time.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: pHash: hashing the low frequencies of a DCT
question: Your service computes pHash with library X; a partner sends pHashes computed with library Y for the same images. Distances between matching pairs are around 30 of 64. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The partner's images were heavily edited
Hamming distance is undefined across libraries
pHash is random by design
Libraries differ in details such as resize filter, mean versus median and whether DC is included, so their bits are not comparable
explain: pHash is a family of variants. Krawetz uses a mean without DC, ImageHash a median with DC, and resampling filters differ too. Meta's PDQ documentation (PDQ is Meta's open-source 256-bit perceptual hash, the subject of lesson 5) makes the same point: even one algorithm in different languages can give different hashes, so it defines conformance against the reference implementation.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: The three contracts: policy, generation and environment interfaces
question: You write a custom environment that runs unit tests. It returns `rewards` as a dict `{"tests": ..., "style": ...}`. GDPO training fails to find the components. What is the most likely bug?
options: Environments may only return a single Tensor
The keys must use the reward/ prefix, for example reward/tests
Rewards must be Python lists, not tensors
Multi-reward environments must set terminateds to all zeros
explain: The environments guide states that each key of a multi-reward dict must use the reward/ prefix. The rollout then stores the summed total_reward and each named component for GDPO.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Colocated vs non-colocated generation, and how weights are refit
question: A single node has 8 GPUs. You set colocated.enabled: false and colocated.resources.gpus_per_node: 8. What happens?
options: Training and generation each get 8 GPUs
Setup fails because training would get 8 - 8 = 0 GPUs
NeMo RL falls back to colocated mode
Generation gets 4 and training gets 4
explain: On one node, training gets cluster.gpus_per_node minus the inference GPUs. The setup asserts that the result is greater than 0, so this config is rejected.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Where the attacker stands: on-path, off-path and on your LAN
question: A host 3,000 km away sends a packet with a forged source address to your server. Which statement is true?
options: It is on-path, because its packet reached your server
It will receive your server's reply, because the source address is in the packet
It cannot reach your server at all without being on the same LAN
It cannot see the reply, so any secret your server puts in the reply (such as a sequence number) must be guessed
explain: Replies go to the forged address, not to the sender. That is the defining limit of an off-path attacker, and why protocols put unguessable values (TCP sequence numbers, DNS transaction IDs) in places only the real peer can see.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: DNS cache poisoning: the race and the birthday maths
question: Why does a forged reply need to arrive before the real one?
options: Because the first reply that passes the checks completes the query, and the real answer arriving later is dropped
Because the resolver checks timestamps
Because UDP delivers only one packet per port
Because the real server would detect the forgery
explain: Once a matching reply is accepted the query is no longer pending, so the later genuine reply has nothing to match and is discarded. The attacker is racing the real server, and only the attacker knows a race is happening.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: RPKI and route origin validation
question: Why does RFC 6811 call origin validation mainly protection against misconfiguration?
options: Because a deliberate attacker can forge a path ending in the authorised origin AS, which ROV accepts
Because ROAs are unsigned
Because ROV only works for IPv6
Because routers ignore Invalid routes by default
explain: ROV checks the last AS in the path and nothing else. A careful attacker appends the legitimate origin to their announcement. Accidental hijacks, such as the 2008 YouTube event, carry the wrong origin and are caught.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Scanning, as defenders see it
question: In conn.log you see thousands of records from one internal workstation, each to a different internal IP on port 445, nearly all with history S and state S0. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: Normal file sharing
The workstation's antivirus updating
A horizontal scan from a possibly compromised internal host; most targets did not answer
A SYN flood against the workstation
explain: One source, one port, many destinations, almost no answers: a horizontal scan, the pattern of worms and of attackers moving laterally. That it comes from inside makes it urgent; isolate and examine the workstation.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Intrusion detection, network monitoring, and where to practise
question: A Suricata sensor is connected to a switch's mirror port. A rule with action 'drop' matches an attack. What happens?
options: Nothing is blocked: a passive sensor sees copies of traffic, so it can alert but not stop the original packets
The rule fails to load
The attack packets are dropped
The switch shuts the port
explain: A sensor on a mirror (spanning) port is passive by definition: it receives copies. Blocking requires an inline deployment where traffic must pass through the sensor, as NIST SP 800-94 describes.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Wireshark display filters: asking precise questions of packets
question: A filter `http.user_agent matches "python"` shows packets whose User-Agent is 'Python-urllib/3.12'. A colleague expected it not to match because of the capital P. Who is right and why?
options: The colleague: matches is case-sensitive like grep
You: matches is case-insensitive by default in Wireshark; add (?-i) to make it case-sensitive
Neither: matches only works on numbers
The colleague: User-Agent values are always lower-cased by the dissector
explain: The manual says matches applies a PCRE2 (Perl Compatible Regular Expressions) pattern that is case-insensitive by default, and shows (?-i) to force case sensitivity. contains, by contrast, compares exact bytes.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Suricata in depth: how rules match, EVE output and tuning
question: An alert fired on an HTTP response. In eve.json, how do you find that same connection's HTTP request, file information and byte counts?
options: Search for the same signature ID
Select every record with the alert's flow_id
Search for the same timestamp
Read fast.log, which contains the full request
explain: Suricata gives all records about one flow the same flow_id; its EVE documentation shows jq selecting on flow_id to gather the alert, http, fileinfo, anomaly and flow events together. A signature ID matches every flow that triggered the rule, and timestamps differ between event types.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Finding beacons with robust statistics: the RITA approach
question: Your beacon report's top entry: 2,800 internal hosts each contact the same destination every 3,600 seconds exactly, with identical response sizes. What is the best conclusion?
options: A company-wide compromise: isolate all 2,800 hosts
Almost certainly managed software checking for updates or reporting telemetry; verify the destination and owner, then allowlist it so real outliers surface
A DNS tunnel
Capture loss on the sensor
explain: Very high prevalence plus perfect regularity is the signature of software deployed everywhere, such as an updater. Confirm what it is (destination owner, process on one host) and allowlist it. A real implant usually shows the opposite pattern: regular timing to a destination that only one or a few hosts ever contact.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: From bits on a wire to packets
question: A packet's header says it comes from address A. What does that prove about who sent it?
options: It proves the packet came from A, because routers check the sender
It proves the packet came from A's network, but not which device
Nothing by itself: the sender's own software wrote that field
It proves the packet came from A only if the payload is longer than the header
explain: The header is just bytes written by whoever built the packet. Some networks filter packets with impossible source addresses (you will meet this as ingress filtering), but the basic protocols do not verify the sender. Treat a source address as a claim, not a proof.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Routing: gateways, TTL, traceroute and BGP
question: A router has routes for `208.65.152.0/22` (to A), `208.65.153.0/24` (to B) and `0.0.0.0/0` (to C). Where does it send a packet for `208.65.155.4`?
options: B, because /24 is the longest prefix in the table
C, because only exact matches count
A, because 208.65.155.4 is inside the /22 (152.0 to 155.255) but not inside the /24
It drops the packet as ambiguous
explain: Longest prefix match only chooses among prefixes that actually contain the address. 208.65.152.0/22 spans 208.65.152.0 to 208.65.155.255, so it matches; the /24 covers only 208.65.153.x. The default route also matches but is shorter.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTP: requests, responses, headers and cookies
question: A log shows 3,000 requests in two minutes from one IP, almost all `404 Not Found`, for paths like `/admin`, `/backup.zip`, `/.git/config`. What is most likely happening?
options: A user with a broken bookmark
Automated scanning for forgotten or sensitive files
A denial-of-service attack using amplification
Normal search engine indexing
explain: Thousands of guessed paths in a short time, mostly missing, are the fingerprint of a content discovery scanner looking for admin panels, backups and exposed repositories. The rare 200 among them is the line to investigate first.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
question: A 4-node server's distance table shows 10 on the diagonal and 20 everywhere else. What is the safest reading?
options: Every remote access costs exactly twice a local one
Remote access is roughly twice as costly as local, but firmware tables can be inaccurate, so measure
The machine is actually UMA because all remote entries are equal
explain: SLIT values are relative estimates normalized to 10 for local access. Drepper shows a real table that reported 20 for every pair even though some pairs had to be two hops apart. Use the table as a hint and benchmark when placement matters.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
question: A database pins each worker to one node and places every buffer with explicit mbind policies. Profiling shows time spent in page faults on pages that never move. What is the most likely fix?
options: Enable MPOL_INTERLEAVE on all buffers
Use smaller pages so faults are cheaper
Disable automatic NUMA balancing for this workload
explain: These are NUMA hinting faults from automatic balancing sampling pages that are already correctly placed. The kernel docs recommend disabling balancing when the workload is already bound to NUMA nodes.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance
question: A service writes 300 TB per year to a 1 TB drive rated for 10,000 P/E cycles. The drive's FDP statistics show media bytes written are 5x host bytes. Roughly how long until rated wear-out?
options: About 6.7 years
About 33 years
About 1.3 years
Never, wear leveling prevents it
explain: Lifetime host writes = 1 TB x 10,000 / 5 = 2,000 TB. At 300 TB per year that is 2000/300, about 6.7 years. Halving A to 2.5 would double it.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
question: Why does DETR not need NMS at test time?
options: Its object queries are fixed to non-overlapping image regions
It applies NMS inside the transformer decoder
One-to-one Hungarian matching during training gives each object only one positive prediction, so other slots learn to predict 'no object'
It only predicts one object per image
explain: Object queries are learned embeddings, not fixed regions. Because the matching assigns each ground-truth object to exactly one slot, a second slot covering the same object is trained toward the no-object class. The DETR paper reports that adding NMS helps early decoder layers but slightly hurts AP at the last layer.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Batching writes: the cost versus latency dial
question: To cut latency further, an engineer changes the Agent to acknowledge a Produce request as soon as it lands in the in-memory buffer. What does this break?
options: Ordering within a partition
Nothing, since S3 is durable
Compaction, because files get smaller
Durability: if the Agent crashes before the PUT, acknowledged records are lost
explain: The buffer is memory in a stateless process. WarpStream never acknowledges a write until it is in object storage and committed to the metadata store, which is what lets it lose every Agent without losing acknowledged data. Acking from memory turns a crash into data loss.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
question: Checkout p99 reads 1.3 s and the orders database p99 reads 0.9 s, both rising in the same minute. What do the metrics alone establish?
options: That checkout requests are waiting on the database
That the database is the root cause, since it is the deepest component
That the two are correlated in time, but not that any single checkout request waited on the database
Nothing, because percentiles from different services are never comparable
explain: Metrics are per-component aggregates with no request identity, so simultaneity is a hypothesis, not a causal link. The slow checkout requests and the slow queries may even be disjoint sets. A trace carries parent and child spans and settles it for one request.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Finding text: EAST geometry maps and DBNet's learnable threshold
question: Why does DBNet replace the hard threshold with a sigmoid of k(P - T)?
options: It makes inference faster than a comparison
It lets gradients flow so the network can learn a per-pixel threshold map
It removes the need for the probability map
It guarantees that adjacent words never merge
explain: A step function has zero gradient almost everywhere, so a threshold inside it cannot be learned. The steep sigmoid approximates the step but stays differentiable. At inference the paper actually drops this path and uses a constant threshold on P.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The kernel/user boundary: rings and the system call door
question: Which bug is usually the most severe for a multi-user Linux server?
options: A crash in a user's text editor
A memory bug in a kernel system call that any process can make
A memory bug in a setuid program that only root can run
A typo in a log message
explain: A kernel bug reachable from any process can bypass every permission check, for every user and every container on the host. A setuid program that only root can run gives an attacker nothing new.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: AppArmor: path-based profiles that confine one program
question: What is the key design difference between AppArmor and SELinux?
options: AppArmor confines users, SELinux confines programs
AppArmor only works on Windows
AppArmor rules name paths a program uses; SELinux rules name types stored in labels on subjects and objects
SELinux is discretionary and AppArmor is mandatory
explain: Both are mandatory and both confine programs. AppArmor writes rules in terms of paths, which makes profiles readable; SELinux writes them in terms of types, so a file's label travels with it.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Namespaces and cgroups: the building blocks of containers
question: A process is root inside a user namespace (mapped to UID 1000 outside). It tries to set the system's calendar clock. What happens?
options: It changes the clock only for the container
It succeeds, because it has all capabilities in its namespace
It succeeds only inside a time namespace
It fails, because capabilities in a user namespace apply only to resources governed by that namespace, and the system clock is not one
explain: user_namespaces(7) uses this very example: changing the system time is governed by CAP_SYS_TIME in the initial namespace. Time namespaces offset only the boot and monotonic clocks.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Secure boot, module signing and kernel hardening knobs
question: An attacker has root on a server with kernel lockdown enabled and module signature enforcement on. What stops them loading a rootkit module they compiled?
options: Secure boot scans the disk at runtime
The rootkit must be in /lib/modules
The kernel refuses modules that are not validly signed with a trusted key, even for root
Nothing: root can do anything
explain: With enforcement, the kernel itself checks the signature at load time. Root controls the filesystem but does not hold the signing key, so the module is refused.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: What OSINT is, and what it is for
question: Under the Berkeley Protocol, which of these is closed-source information?
options: A company's published annual report
A satellite image anyone can buy from a commercial provider
Details an investigator learns by messaging an employee on a social network
A public video on a video-sharing site
explain: The Protocol treats information acquired "through communication with" internet users as closed source. Buying satellite imagery is fine: open source includes what the public can purchase.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Search operators: asking a search engine precise questions
question: A `site:northwind.example filetype:pdf` search returns nothing. What can you conclude?
options: Northwind has no PDF files on any server
Google has not shown any indexed PDFs for that query; others may exist or be unindexed
Northwind blocks Google entirely
The query syntax was wrong
explain: Google documents that site: results are not always exhaustive. An empty result is evidence about the index, not about the server.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Verifying images and claims: provenance, reposts and hashes
question: Why can a SHA-256 hash not find a resized repost of a photo, while dHash can?
options: SHA-256 is too slow for images
